positions.claim: US AI leadership requires both a closed and an open-source ecosystem, and support for open source is the first item in chapter one of the administration's AI Action Plan.
Hard regulatory red lines for AI do not survive contact with the frontier; the EU AI Act was finalized before ChatGPT existed and now governs LLMs it never anticipated.
The prior administration's fixed compute threshold for mandatory government disclosure was a mistake of the same kind, and this administration is deliberately cautious about setting such thresholds.
Once government sets a regulatory line it is very hard to reset, so the cost of setting one too early is higher than the cost of waiting.
Biological risk from AI models has been overblown for years — warnings began in 2021-22 and it has not been an issue for three years — while cyber capability is the more real present risk.
Test and eval infrastructure for models crossing the frontier still needs to be built, even if current risk claims are overstated.
A state-by-state patchwork of AI regulation functions as a subsidy to large incumbents, who can absorb the legal cost, and as a barrier to startups who cannot.
A single national AI standard passed by Congress would be the single biggest regulatory boon available to startups.
No administration in history has been more committed to reducing regulations than the current one.
Regulatory strategy should differ by category: preserve the unregulated state of 'born free' technologies and aggressively remove approval barriers for 'born in captivity' ones.
Supersonic flight is the clearest example of technological stagnation caused by rules — the fix is regulating noise rather than speed over the United States.

The Vannevar Bush model of federal science funding is outdated because the funding shares inverted: government fell from ~70% of R&D in 1950 to ~30%, with private sector plus philanthropy now at ~70% and near parity in basic research.

AI will fundamentally change how scientific discovery is done within two to three years across materials science, pharmaceuticals, and chemistry, and the ~$200B/year federal R&D budget should be prioritized accordingly.
The government's role is to shape the arena rather than direct discovery, leaving robotics for cloud labs and hypothesis-generation software as startup territory.

Quantum information science is where AI was in 2017-18 in Washington — underdiscussed relative to its importance — and the administration is targeting a scientifically relevant quantum computer at DOE by 2028.
Executive orders are a weaker instrument than statute because a successor administration can simply revoke them, which is why preemption should be legislated.
Model outputs that reproduce protected IP such as Mickey Mouse should be prohibited, and that prohibition should be clarified in statute.
Creator licensing and revenue-sharing markets for AI training should be left to mature on their own rather than legislated now.
Founder and startup-community pressure on Washington — like the week's open-weights letters — improves policy outcomes rather than merely creating noise.
